summary: Defines several additional features for PPP's Link Control Protocol, suggested over the years, used to establish, configure, and test a data link connection.

eli5.summary: PPP has a part that sets up the line. This memo adds extra options that people kept asking for.

questions: what is the ppp callback option
subtitle: Two new LCP packets and four new options for PPP: identify yourself, announce time left, change the FCS, pad, call back and bundle frames.

tldr.problem: PPP's Link Control Protocol handles setting up and testing a link, but people had asked for extra features over the years, such as a way to identify the peer, alternatives to the default frame check, and fewer frames during setup.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds two LCP packet codes (Identification, Time-Remaining) and four configuration options (FCS-Alternatives, Self-Describing-Padding, Callback, Compound-Frames), each negotiated through normal LCP exchanges.
tldr.outcome: PPP implementations gain optional features for troubleshooting, session timing, cheaper checksumming, dial-back and bundled frames. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1548 and is itself updated by RFC 2484.

today: RFC 1570 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1548, and it is itself updated by RFC 2484. Read the two together for the current form of these LCP extensions.

sections.title: What This RFC Adds to LCP
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) carries multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links, and its Link Control Protocol (LCP) establishes, configures and tests the link. RFC 1570 defines additional LCP features suggested over the previous few years. It builds on the packet and option formats already defined in RFC 1548.

Two new LCP Codes are added: 12 (Identification) and 13 (Time-Remaining). Four new Configuration Option types are added: 9 (FCS-Alternatives), 10 (Self-Describing-Padding), 13 (Callback) and 15 (Compound-Frames). The RFC points to the Assigned Numbers RFC for the up-to-date values.
sections.eli5: PPP already has a way to set up a line between two machines. This paper hands out a few extra tools for that setup.

sections.title: Identification and Time-Remaining Packets
sections.content:
Identification lets an implementation tell its peer who it is, for uses like link troubleshooting or license enforcement. It may be sent at any time, even before LCP reaches the Opened state, and it gets no response. The RFC recommends sending it when a Configure-Reject is sent or received, as a final message if negotiation fails to converge, and when LCP reaches the Opened state. It is a separate Code rather than an option so it is available as early as the Link Establishment phase, when non-LCP packets cannot be sent.

Time-Remaining tells the peer how long the session has left. It is advisory only: the session actually ends with a Terminate-Request. It may only be sent in the LCP Opened state and is expected from one side, generally a network access server. Its Seconds-Remaining field is a 32-bit unsigned value, and 0xffffffff means no timeout.

Both packets carry the sender's Magic-Number (zero until the Magic-Number option has been negotiated) and a free-form Message. The Message is meant to be human-readable, preferably ASCII characters 32 through 126, and must not affect how the protocol operates. The Identifier must change for each packet sent. A Code-Reject of either packet should generate the RXJ+ (permitted) event.
sections.eli5: Identification is a name tag a machine can show its partner. Time-Remaining is a clock that says how many seconds are left before the call ends.

sections.title: FCS-Alternatives
sections.content:
The FCS-Alternatives option lets a side ask the peer to use a different frame check sequence, or to drop the FCS altogether. It is negotiated separately in each direction, and the negotiated values apply only in the Authentication and Network-Layer Protocol phases. Frames in any other phase must use the default FCS. The one-octet Options field is a logical OR of 1 (Null FCS), 2 (CCITT 16-bit FCS) and 4 (CCITT 32-bit FCS). For most PPP HDLC links the default is the CCITT 16-bit FCS.

When LCP renegotiates or terminates, it is recommended that the Configure-Request or Terminate-Request be sent first with the last negotiated FCS and then again with the default FCS. On receiving either request, an implementation must switch to the default FCS for sending and receiving. The RFC mentions a single 48-bit FCS combining the 16-bit and 32-bit forms but did not standardize it because of intellectual property concerns.

The Null FCS should only be used for protocols with an end-to-end checksum, such as TCP/IP or UDP/IP with the checksum enabled. Configuration and authentication packets must always include the FCS and must have it verified. Appendix A gives C code for computing the 32-bit FCS with a lookup table.
sections.eli5: Every frame ends with a check number that shows whether it got scrambled. This option lets two machines agree on a stronger check, or skip it when something else already does the checking.

sections.title: Self-Describing Padding
sections.content:
The Self-Describing-Padding option says a side understands padding that describes itself. It matters when protocols such as network-layer or compression protocols need trailing padding detected and removed. If the option is rejected, the peer must not add padding to the identified special protocols. If it is acknowledged, the peer must follow the self-describing procedure for them.

Each pad octet holds its own index. The first pad octet must be 1, and after the FCS is removed the final pad octet gives the number of pad octets to remove, so three pad octets hold 1, 2, 3. The option's Maximum field is the Maximum-Pad-Value, from 1 to 255, with 2, 4 or 8 the most likely. If no padding is needed but the last octet of the Information field is between 1 and that maximum, at least one pad octet must be added. A frame with a wrong pad index should be silently discarded.
sections.eli5: If a box has empty space, each filler piece is numbered 1, 2, 3. The last number tells the receiver how many filler pieces to throw away.

sections.title: Callback
sections.content:
The Callback option lets one side ask a dial-up peer to call it back, for example to save on toll charges. Once it is negotiated and authentication completes, the link goes straight to the Termination phase and is disconnected. The peer then re-establishes the link without negotiating Callback.

The Operation octet says what the Message holds: 0 for a location set by user authentication, 1 for a dialing string, 2 for a location identifier used with authentication for a database lookup, 3 for an E.164 number and 4 for a distinguished name. A peer that agrees to Callback should also request the Authentication-Protocol option, since user information learned during authentication can set or limit the callback location, or decide whom to bill.
sections.eli5: It is like asking a friend to hang up and ring you back, so the call is on their phone bill. First they check it really is you.

sections.title: Compound-Frames
sections.content:
The Compound-Frames option lets a sender pack several PPP packets into one frame, which can save on toll charges. Only protocols with a determinate length or an integral length field may be aggregated. Each packet is followed by another Protocol field and its datagram. The option must be negotiated together with Self-Describing-Padding, and if FCS-Alternatives was negotiated, self-describing padding must always be added.

On receipt, the first Protocol field is handled as usual and the rest of the frame goes back to the demultiplexor. Processing stops when a packet without a determinate length is handled, when the frame is empty, or when a Protocol field with the value 1 is found. That value is reserved as the Padding Protocol, and everything after it is removed as padding.

The option can cut negotiation latency. The first Configure-Request is sent normally in one frame, including both options. The peer should answer with a Configure-Ack followed, in a compound frame, by its own Configure-Request and any NCP Configure-Requests. With the peer's final return frame, the minimum number of frames to finish configuration is 4.
sections.eli5: Instead of mailing three letters in three envelopes, you put them in one envelope. The receiver reads one after another until it finds the filler.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says only that security issues are briefly discussed in the sections about the Callback option. Those sections note that Callback should be paired with authentication, and that only an authorized user is expected to have the correct site-specific information to use the Callback message. The range of allowed use of that field is outside the scope of the specification.
sections.eli5: The only safety advice is about calling back: make sure the person asking is really allowed to ask.

fields.name: Identifier
fields.desc: Must change for each packet sent.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: At least 12; the Message field follows the fixed part.

fields.name: Magic-Number
fields.desc: Zero until the Magic-Number option is negotiated.

fields.name: Seconds-Remaining
fields.desc: Seconds left in the session; 0xffffffff means forever.

items.label: Null FCS
items.desc: No FCS; only for protocols with an end-to-end checksum.

items.label: CCITT 16-bit FCS
items.desc: The usual default for PPP HDLC framed links.

items.label: CCITT 32-bit FCS
items.desc: A longer check; values are combined by logical OR.

items.label: Dialing string
items.desc: Format depends on the device making the callback.

items.label: Location identifier
items.desc: Used with authentication information for a database lookup.

items.label: Distinguished name
items.desc: A name identifying the callback location.
